title: How Would You Migrate This System to a New Architecture While It's Serving Live Traffic?
summary: The hardest applied brownfield question — tests whether you can sequence a live migration and name what you'd monitor to know it's safe to proceed at each stage.

slides.markdown:
The interviewer asks: **"how would you migrate this system to a new architecture while it's serving live traffic?"** "Just switch over one weekend" isn't a viable answer at this level — it ignores that a mistake discovered at 100% cutover has no graceful way back.

A strong answer sequences the migration in stages — shadow, dual-write, phased cutover — and names what you'd monitor at each gate to know it's safe to proceed.

Ask whether any downtime can be tolerated at all, and what the rollback point is if the new system misbehaves. Is the hard part the data migration, the traffic cutover, or both?

The rollback question in particular shapes the whole plan — a migration with a clean rollback point at every stage can move faster than one where certain steps, once taken, can't be undone.

Shadow the new system with live traffic first, then dual-write, then phase reads over, verifying at each gate before proceeding.

Each stage exists to catch a different kind of problem before it has real user-facing impact — shadowing catches correctness issues with zero risk, dual-write catches write-path issues while reads are still safe, and phased reads catch anything left over at a small, contained blast radius.

![Four-stage migration pipeline: shadow, dual-write, phased cutover, decommission, gated by verification](assets/migration-pipeline-stages.svg)

A live migration staged as shadow to dual-write to phased read cutover to decommission old. Each arrow between stages is a gate, not a formality — proceeding past it requires the previous stage's verification to actually pass.

This is the shape every answer to this question should follow, regardless of the specific system being migrated.

assets.alt: Four-stage migration pipeline: shadow, dual-write, phased cutover, decommission, gated by verification

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: migrating an orders database to a sharded design
slides.markdown:
A concrete scenario: migrating an orders database from a monolithic Postgres instance to a sharded design. Stage one, the new sharded store is written to in shadow alongside the real writes, with nothing reading from it yet. Stage two, a small percentage of reads are served from the new store and diffed against the old store's answer for the same query. Stage three, once the diff rate is near zero for a sustained window, reads are phased over fully. Stage four, the old store is decommissioned only after a safety window with zero incidents.

Each stage narrows the blast radius of any remaining bug before it's ever exposed to more than a small slice of real traffic.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: what verifying at each gate actually means
slides.markdown:
What "verifying at each gate" actually means concretely: an automated diff rate threshold — for example, proceed only if mismatches stay under 0.01% over 48 hours — not a subjective "looks good" call from the team.

Naming a specific number and window here is what separates a real gate from a rubber stamp; without it, "verify before proceeding" is just a slide title with no actual mechanism behind it.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
This staged approach is far slower than a cutover weekend and costs real engineering time running two systems and a diffing pipeline in parallel. That cost buys you the ability to catch a correctness or performance problem while it's still low-blast-radius, instead of discovering it at 100% cutover.

The trade is speed against blast radius — a weekend cutover is fast when it works and catastrophic when it doesn't; a staged migration is slow but converts a possible catastrophe into a contained, recoverable incident.

Follow-up: "the new system's data has drifted from the old one mid-migration — how do you catch that?" The same diffing pipeline used to gate the cutover, run continuously during the dual-write period, not just as a one-time check before flipping reads.

Drift detection isn't a separate mechanism bolted on for this scenario — it's the same gate infrastructure, simply run continuously rather than as a single pass/fail checkpoint.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: a schema difference that can't dual-write identically
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "how do you handle a schema difference between old and new that can't be dual-written identically?" A translation layer at the write path maps the old shape to the new one during the transition, accepting that layer as temporary migration-only complexity that gets deleted once the old system is decommissioned.

Naming it explicitly as temporary and scheduled for deletion is what keeps this translation layer from quietly becoming permanent, unmaintained complexity.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: cutting over all at once
slides.markdown:
**Wrong move:** cutting over all traffic at once "since testing looked good," with no staged, gated verification against real production data and traffic.

**Why it's wrong:** staging environments and test data rarely reproduce the actual shape and volume of production traffic — a problem invisible in testing can appear only under real load, and a full cutover exposes it to 100% of users simultaneously with no gradual detection.

**Correct model:** always stage the cutover through shadow, dual-write, and phased reads, gated by measured thresholds against real traffic.

Stage the migration as shadow, then dual-write, then phased read cutover, then decommission — gated at each step by a measured threshold against real production traffic, not a subjective sign-off. Run the same diffing pipeline continuously during dual-write to catch drift, not just as a one-time check.

Name the trade-off explicitly: this is far slower than a weekend cutover, but it converts a possible catastrophic failure into a contained, recoverable incident.
